help.title: What should the PGN look like?
help.intro: Each exercise is one game in the file: a starting position and a line of moves. The first move is the opponent's and is played for you; the rest is the solution you have to find.
help.rule1: An exercise is a block of bracketed tags followed by its moves. Leave a blank line between exercises.
help.rule2: The [FEN] is the position BEFORE the opponent's move. If you take the exercise from a game, it is the position just before the opponent's mistake.
help.rule3: The line starts with the opponent's move and continues with your solution, alternating: opponent, you, opponent, you… It must end on one of your moves.
help.rule4: Only the main line counts: variations, comments and symbols are ignored. Moves use standard notation (Nf3, exd5, O-O, e8=Q).
help.tagFen: the position before the opponent's move. Without it the starting position is used.
help.tagThemes: optional: themes separated by spaces, like fork or mateIn2. Catalogue themes show with their translated name.
help.lichess: Does your position already start with your turn, like in a Lichess study? Use the FEN from one move earlier and put the opponent's last move first.

hangingPiece.idea: An undefended piece can be captured for free
hangingPiece.see: Look at the black knight: no piece protects it.
hangingPiece.play: The bishop captures it with no risk.
hangingPiece.why: A free piece! If nobody defends it, nobody can recapture.
hangingPiece.tip: Before every move ask yourself: which enemy pieces are undefended?

mateIn1.idea: Checkmate: the king has no escape
mateIn1.see: The black king is in the corner. Count its free squares.
mateIn1.play: The queen gives check from g7, protected by our king.
mateIn1.why: It cannot capture the queen or flee: checkmate!
mateIn1.tip: Look for checks the king can neither capture nor dodge.

fork.idea: One piece attacks two at once, and only one can be saved
fork.see: The black king and rook can be attacked from the same square: d6.
fork.play: The knight jumps to d6, attacking both.
fork.why: The king must escape the check and the rook falls: a fork!
fork.tip: Knights are the kings of forks: look for squares that attack two pieces.

pin.idea: A piece can't move because it would expose a more valuable one
pin.see: The black knight is on the same file as its king.
pin.why: If the knight moves, the rook captures the king: it is pinned and cannot escape.
pin.tip: Attack the pinned piece with more pieces: it can't run away.

skewer.idea: You attack a valuable piece; when it steps aside, the one behind falls
skewer.see: The black king and rook are on the same rank.
skewer.play: The rook gives check to the king.
skewer.play2: The king has to step aside...
skewer.play3: ...and the rook captures the piece behind it.
skewer.why: A skewer! The valuable piece goes first, then the other falls.
skewer.tip: It's a pin in reverse: the valuable piece is in front.

discoveredAttack.idea: Moving one piece unmasks the attack of another behind it
discoveredAttack.see: The bishop blocks the rook's file. At the end of that file stands the black queen.
discoveredAttack.play: The bishop captures with check: the king must respond.
discoveredAttack.play2: The black king takes the bishop...
discoveredAttack.play3: ...and the rook, no longer blocked, captures the queen.
discoveredAttack.why: A discovered attack! Two threats at once and only one can be stopped.
discoveredAttack.tip: Look for your own pieces that block your rook, bishop or queen.

doubleCheck.idea: Two pieces give check at once: the king can only move
doubleCheck.see: The white knight blocks the rook's file, and the rook points at the black king.
doubleCheck.play: The knight moves and gives check, unmasking the rook's check too.
doubleCheck.why: You can't block or capture two pieces at once: the king must run.
doubleCheck.tip: Double check is the strongest move: look for a discovered check that also checks.

backRankMate.idea: The king is trapped on its back rank by its own pawns
backRankMate.see: The black king's pawns block all its exits.
backRankMate.play: The rook enters the back rank with check.
backRankMate.why: The king can't flee or capture the rook: back-rank mate!
backRankMate.tip: Always give your king an exit: push a pawn to make a luft.

trappedPiece.idea: An attacked piece with no safe square to go to
trappedPiece.see: Look at the black knight on a8: its exits (b6 and c7) are covered.
trappedPiece.why: Trapped! Every square it can reach is attacked.
trappedPiece.then: The king moves, and the bishop captures the trapped knight.
trappedPiece.tip: Pieces on the edge get trapped easily: count their exit squares.

smotheredMate.idea: The king is smothered by its own pieces and a knight gives check
smotheredMate.see: The black king is surrounded by its rook and pawns.
smotheredMate.play: The knight jumps to f7 with check.
smotheredMate.why: A knight's check can't be blocked and the king has no squares: smothered mate!
smotheredMate.tip: Knight checks can't be blocked: use them when the king is boxed in.

mateIn2.idea: Mate in two: first box the king in, then deliver mate
mateIn2.see: Two rooks against the king in the corner.
mateIn2.play: One rook cuts off the 7th rank: the king can't step down.
mateIn2.play2: The king can only go to g8...
mateIn2.play3: ...and the other rook delivers mate on the 8th rank.
mateIn2.why: One rook cuts, the other finishes: ladder mate!
mateIn2.tip: Think two moves ahead: which move leaves the king with no squares?

capturingDefender.idea: Capture the piece that defends another, and that one is left unprotected
capturingDefender.see: The e5 pawn is protected only by the knight on c6.
capturingDefender.play: The bishop captures the knight that was protecting the pawn.
capturingDefender.why: Without its defender, the e5 pawn hangs!
capturingDefender.play3: ...and the white knight takes the e5 pawn, now unprotected.
capturingDefender.tip: Ask yourself: who defends that piece? Can I remove the defender?

deflection.idea: You force a piece to leave its defensive post
deflection.see: The black king is the only defender of the rook on g6.
deflection.play: The pawn promotes with check. The king must capture the queen...
deflection.why: Deflected! The king moved away and the rook lost its defender.
deflection.then: The white king captures the rook.
deflection.tip: Find the piece that holds another one up and force it away with a check or capture.

attraction.idea: You lure a piece (often the king) to a square where you can punish it
attraction.see: The a7 pawn is one step from promoting, but the black rook watches the 8th rank.
attraction.play: We sacrifice the rook on e8 with check.
attraction.play2: The king captures and lands on e8...
attraction.play3: ...and the pawn promotes with check: we win.
attraction.why: The king was lured to the fatal square.
attraction.tip: A sacrifice can be bait: ask what happens if the piece captures it.

xRayAttack.idea: A piece attacks "through" another, as if seeing inside
xRayAttack.see: The white rook on g7 stands right behind the black rook on g5.
xRayAttack.play: The pawn gives check from g4.
xRayAttack.play2: The black rook captures it: it has no other move.
xRayAttack.play3: The white rook captures the black one: it saw through the other.
xRayAttack.why: X-ray! The g7 rook supported g4 despite the pieces in between.
xRayAttack.tip: When counting attackers and defenders, count the pieces behind too.

intermezzo.idea: An in-between move (often a check) before the expected capture
intermezzo.see: Our rook is attacked by the bishop, and the pawn could capture the black rook.
intermezzo.play: Before capturing, check with the rook: the opponent has no time to take it.
intermezzo.play3: ...and now the pawn captures the rook.
intermezzo.why: An in-between move! A check saved our rook.
intermezzo.tip: Before recapturing, look for a check or a bigger threat.

arabianMate.idea: Rook and knight trap the king in the corner
arabianMate.see: The king is on h8. The knight watches g8 and h7.
arabianMate.play: The rook gives check from h7, protected by the knight.
arabianMate.why: The king can't capture the rook or flee: Arabian mate!
arabianMate.tip: With the enemy king in the corner, coordinate rook and knight.

anastasiaMate.idea: Knight and rook mate, with the king's own pawn blocking its escape
anastasiaMate.see: The king has its pawn next to it, and the knight watches g8 and g6.
anastasiaMate.play: The rook gives check along the h-file.
anastasiaMate.why: The black pawn blocks its exit and there are no more squares: Anastasia's mate!
anastasiaMate.tip: Look for mates on the edge when the king has a pawn beside it.

bodenMate.idea: Two crossing bishops mate the king on the queenside
bodenMate.see: The black king is blocked by its own pieces.
bodenMate.play: The bishop checks from a6; the other covers c7 and b8.
bodenMate.why: The diagonals cross and there is no escape: Boden's mate!
bodenMate.tip: Two bishops on crossing diagonals control lots of squares.

hookMate.idea: Rook, knight and pawn work together to mate beside the king's own pawn
hookMate.see: The black king has its own pawn beside it. Look at the white knight and pawn.
hookMate.play: The rook checks from f8, protected by the knight.
hookMate.why: The king can't capture the rook or step to h7 or f7: hook mate!
hookMate.tip: The pawn protects the knight and the knight protects the rook: a chain that shuts every exit.
